How to read this. Exposure is the share of an occupation’s tasks where an LLM like GPT-4 could cut the time to complete them by at least half. It measures potential, not a job-loss forecast — high exposure can mean augmentation as readily as displacement. Figures are built bottom-up from all 1,035 ANZSCO occupations, each mapped to a US SOC code carrying scores from Eloundou et al., then aggregated up to sub-industries and industries.
Occupation
The kind of work a person does, regardless of where they do it — e.g. accountant, truck driver, software engineer. Exposure is measured at this level, because AI acts on tasks, and tasks belong to occupations.
Industry
The kind of business a person works for, regardless of their role — e.g. banking, construction, hospitals. Every industry contains a mix of occupations, so its exposure is the blend of the jobs inside it. Divisions (19 broad sectors) split into sub-industries.
Weighted by employment
Each occupation counts in proportion to how many people do it. This answers “how exposed is the average worker?” — the right lens for workforce, skills, and change-management questions.
Weighted by GDP
Each industry counts in proportion to the economic value it produces. This answers “how exposed is the average dollar of output?” — the right lens for productivity and investment questions. It runs higher than the employment view because high-value sectors like finance are also highly exposed.
Sources & caveats. Employment: Stats NZ 2023 Census (Industry by Occupation), randomly rounded to base 3 — summed detail can drift from published sector totals by tens of people. GDP: Stats NZ National Accounts, nominal NZD, year ended March 2024. Exposure scores are US-derived, assuming a similar NZ task mix. Occupation-mapping confidence averages ~77; low-confidence maps are flagged.
Scenario definitions. The three columns of the toggle are the three exposure measures from Eloundou, Manning, Mishkin & Rock (2024), GPTs are GPTs, Science 384:1306–1308 — a spectrum from what AI can do today to what it could do once software catches up.
α AI today
Tasks an LLM can already speed up through a plain chat interface like ChatGPT, with no extra software. The conservative lower bound — what’s in reach right now.
β AI + tools
Adds tasks that open up once AI is paired with everyday tools — things like a spreadsheet, a search engine, or a document editor connected to the model.
ζ AI + software
The upper bound. Counts every task that could be exposed once purpose-built, LLM-powered software is fully developed and deployed. (Labelled “gamma” in some derivations; the paper uses ζ.)
